# OneCoin / “Cryptoqueen” Network: Publicly Documented Fraud Scheme and Enforcement Status

## Executive summary

The available record supports a concrete conclusion: OneCoin was documented by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) as an international investment-fraud scheme that marketed a purported cryptocurrency through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. The scheme operated principally from 2014 through 2019, was based in Sofia, Bulgaria, and generated more than $4 billion in investments from victims worldwide, according to the DOJ. The two principal founders identified in the supplied sources are Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood. The DOJ describes both as co-founders who, together with others, orchestrated the scheme. A legal-industry summary provides additional allegations regarding Greenwood’s operational and financial role, including that he was OneCoin’s top MLM distributor and allegedly earned more than $300 million in commissions. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [S1]; [ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison) [S2])

The enforcement record is materially stronger for Greenwood than for Ignatova. Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to forfeit approximately $300,000, according to the supplied legal summary. The DOJ also states that several key figures connected with OneCoin have been sentenced and that more than $40 million in forfeited assets was available for victim compensation as of April 13, 2026. ([S1]; [S2])

Ruja Ignatova’s status must be described cautiously. The supplied DOJ material identifies her as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and states that law enforcement continues efforts to locate her. The record provided here does not establish that she has been arrested, confirmed dead, or definitively located. Accordingly, “remains at large” is an enforcement-status description supported by the sources—not proof of any particular theory about her whereabouts or fate. ([S1])

## Sources and evidentiary hierarchy

The principal source is the DOJ press release dated April 13, 2026. It is the most authoritative source supplied because it is an official government account of the remission process, the underlying prosecution history, victim losses, asset forfeiture, and the continuing law-enforcement status of Ignatova. ([S1])

The second source is an ArentFox Schiff Investigations Blog article dated September 15, 2023. It summarizes Greenwood’s sentence and several factual allegations drawn from the government’s prosecution. It is useful for details not repeated in the 2026 DOJ remission announcement, but it is a secondary legal commentary source and should be treated as less authoritative than the DOJ’s primary statement. ([S2])

| Source ID | Source | Date | Evidentiary significance |
|---|---|---:|---|
| S1 | U.S. Department of Justice, “Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture” | April 13, 2026 | Primary government source concerning the scheme, victims, forfeiture, remission, and Ignatova’s fugitive status |
| S2 | ArentFox Schiff, “Co-Founder of Fraudulent Cryptocurrency Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison” | September 15, 2023 | Secondary legal summary concerning Greenwood’s sentence, alleged role, compensation structure, and representations made about OneCoin |

## Reconstruction of the OneCoin scheme

### Formation, location, and operating period

According to the DOJ, OneCoin Ltd. began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria. The scheme operated between 2014 and 2019, the period identified by the DOJ for purchases of the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency that may qualify for compensation. ([S1])

The available sources identify Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood as OneCoin’s co-founders. The DOJ states that the pair, together with others, orchestrated an international cryptocurrency investment scheme. This establishes their public identification as principal founders, although the supplied DOJ text does not provide a detailed division of responsibilities between them. ([S1])

Greenwood is further described by the secondary source as a citizen of Sweden and the United Kingdom. The article identifies Ignatova as OneCoin’s other co-founder and states that she remained at large at the time of the article. ([S2])

### Marketing through a global MLM network

OneCoin was marketed and sold through a global MLM network. The structure reportedly provided commissions to members who recruited other individuals to purchase OneCoin packages. This recruitment-based model was central to distribution: rather than relying solely on conventional cryptocurrency-market activity, the scheme used participants and distributors to expand its customer base and generate additional purchases. ([S1]; [S2])

The sources describe OneCoin as a fraudulent cryptocurrency bearing the same name as the company. The DOJ characterizes the scheme as involving misrepresentations about the cryptocurrency and states that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide. ([S1])

The supplied legal summary adds that Greenwood was allegedly OneCoin’s top MLM distributor and allegedly received 5% of monthly OneCoin sales. The article states that those alleged commissions totaled more than $300 million. Because this detail is presented in a secondary account using prosecutorial allegations, it should not be treated as an independently verified accounting of Greenwood’s total proceeds. ([S2])

### Alleged misrepresentations concerning value and technology

The sources identify two central representations that prosecutors alleged were false.

First, OneCoin allegedly represented that its value was determined by market supply and demand. According to the legal summary, prosecutors instead alleged that the value was set arbitrarily and without regard to market forces. This allegation goes to the economic foundation of the product: purchasers were allegedly led to believe that the token had a market-based value when, according to prosecutors, the price was controlled by the scheme. ([S2])

Second, Greenwood allegedly claimed that OneCoin had a private blockchain capable of identifying OneCoins and recording historical transactions. The legal summary states that prosecutors alleged no public, verifiable blockchain actually existed. This allegation concerns the technological legitimacy of the purported cryptocurrency and the ability of investors or outsiders to verify transactions independently. ([S2])

These two allegations should be distinguished from proven adjudicated facts in the supplied material. The DOJ establishes the government’s description of the scheme and the related enforcement process. The ArentFox Schiff article reports what prosecutors alleged regarding the value mechanism and blockchain. The supplied sources do not include a complete indictment, trial verdict, sentencing memorandum, or judicial findings addressing every individual misrepresentation.

## Principal founders and roles

### Ruja Ignatova

The DOJ identifies Ignatova as a co-founder of OneCoin and as one of the individuals who orchestrated the scheme with Greenwood and others. The available record does not specify a complete formal job description for her, such as whether she controlled particular corporate entities, directed marketing operations, or managed specific financial channels. Therefore, the supported characterization is that she was a principal founder and alleged central organizer, not that every more specific operational role has been established by the supplied evidence. ([S1])

Ignatova is also identified as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive. The DOJ states that the FBI continues investigative efforts to locate her. The supplied record does not report an arrest or a confirmed location. ([S1])

### Karl Sebastian Greenwood

Greenwood is identified as OneCoin’s co-founder and as a major participant in its MLM distribution system. The secondary source states that he was the scheme’s top MLM distributor and allegedly earned 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, totaling more than $300 million. ([S2])

Unlike the available record concerning Ignatova, Greenwood’s criminal case reached sentencing. The supplied source states that he was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his role in the fraud scheme and ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. The DOJ separately states that several key figures in OneCoin-related prosecutions have been sentenced. ([S1]; [S2])

The phrase “alleged role” in the secondary article should not obscure the enforcement outcome: the source reports a sentence, meaning that Greenwood’s case resulted in a criminal judgment and punishment. However, the supplied materials do not provide the precise counts of conviction, the sentencing court’s complete findings, or the terms of any restitution order beyond the approximately $300,000 forfeiture figure reported by S2.

## Victims, losses, and recovered assets

The DOJ states that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide. The secondary source states that approximately 3.5 million investors were affected or solicited. These figures are not identical types of measurements: the $4 billion figure describes investment volume or victim investment, while the 3.5 million figure describes the approximate number of investors. The sources do not establish that every investor lost the same proportion of funds or that the full $4 billion represents a proven net-loss calculation. ([S1]; [S2])

The DOJ announced that more than $40 million in forfeited assets was available for victim compensation through a remission process. This amount is substantially smaller than the more than $4 billion in worldwide investments described by the DOJ, demonstrating that the announced recovery represents only a fraction of the reported investment volume. The sources do not state the final amount each eligible victim will receive or whether the $40 million figure will increase. ([S1])

Eligibility is described in the DOJ announcement as relating to individuals who purchased the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency between 2014 and 2019. The remission administrator is Kroll Settlement Administration LLC. The DOJ states that no payment is required to participate and warns victims about impersonation and recovery scams. ([S1])

## Enforcement facts versus unresolved claims

| Issue | Supported enforcement fact | Allegation or unresolved point |
|---|---|---|
| OneCoin’s nature | DOJ characterizes it as a fraudulent cryptocurrency investment scheme | The supplied record does not include every underlying judicial finding |
| Founders | Ignatova and Greenwood are identified as co-founders | The precise division of responsibilities between them is not fully documented in the supplied sources |
| Greenwood | Reported sentence of 20 years and approximately $300,000 forfeiture | The exact conviction counts and complete sentencing findings are not supplied |
| Greenwood’s commissions | Reported allegation of more than $300 million in commissions | The figure is presented through a secondary summary of prosecutorial allegations |
| Blockchain | Prosecutors alleged there was no public, verifiable blockchain | The supplied materials do not include technical records or a judicial analysis of the blockchain issue |
| Investor losses | DOJ reports more than $4 billion invested worldwide | The sources do not quantify verified net losses for each victim |
| Ignatova’s status | DOJ identifies her as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and says efforts continue to locate her | No supplied evidence confirms her death, capture, location, or the truth of any specific disappearance theory |
| Victim recovery | More than $40 million in forfeited assets was available for compensation | The ultimate distribution and individual recovery amounts remain unspecified |

## Assessment of Ruja Ignatova’s status

The responsible assessment is that Ignatova’s status is unresolved in the supplied public record, but her official enforcement status is “at large” or fugitive. The DOJ identifies her as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and describes continuing efforts to locate her. The secondary source similarly states that she remained at large. ([S1]; [S2])

No supplied source establishes that she is dead, living under a particular identity, located in a particular country, or protected by named individuals. Those possibilities must therefore be excluded from a factual reconstruction based only on the available evidence. The absence of a confirmed location is not evidence of death, and the designation “fugitive” is not evidence that law enforcement knows where she is. The strongest supported conclusion is limited: she has not been shown by these sources to have been apprehended, and U.S. authorities continue to seek her.

## Overall conclusion

The publicly documented evidence supports the view that OneCoin was a large-scale, internationally marketed investment-fraud scheme presented as a cryptocurrency enterprise. Its core mechanism combined claims of technological legitimacy and market-based value with a global MLM recruitment structure. Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood are the identified principal founders. Greenwood’s criminal case resulted in a reported 20-year sentence and forfeiture, while Ignatova remains an identified fugitive whose location and ultimate status are not resolved by the supplied sources. ([S1]; [S2])

The DOJ’s 2026 remission announcement is significant because it confirms an active effort to convert forfeited criminal proceeds into compensation for eligible victims. Nevertheless, the more than $40 million identified for remission is far below the more than $4 billion in worldwide investments reported by the DOJ. The compensation process therefore represents partial recovery, not restoration of the victims’ total reported financial exposure. ([S1])

[https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

Benefits DOJ Vacancies Legal Careers at DOJ Our Offices Find Help Contact Us Search Breadcrumb Justice.gov Office of Public Affairs News Press Releases Justice Department Announces Compensation Process For OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture MENU News All News Blogs Photo Galleries Podcasts Press Releases Speeches Videos Archived Press Releases Archived News Press Release Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture Monday, April 13, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Today, the Department of Justice announced the beginning of the remission compensation process to provide recovery for victims of the international investment scheme involving OneCoin Ltd. Between 2014 and 2019, Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood, co-founders of OneCoin Ltd. (OneCoin), and others orchestrated a large, international cryptocurrency investment scheme defrauding investors from around the globe. OneCoin, which began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria, marketed and sold a fraudulent cryptocurrency by the same name through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. As a result of misrepresentations made about OneCoin, victims invested over $4 billion worldwide in the fraudulent cryptocurrency. The Department of Justice filed a number of OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York. Several key figures involved in the scheme have been sentenced, and the Department pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the proceeds of the fraud scheme. More than $40 million in forfeited assets are currently available for victim compensation. Through the remission process, victims who purchased the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency between 2014 and 2019 may be eligible for compensation. Individuals who believe they may be victims may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com . Victims may also call, email, or write to the Remission Administrator to request that a Petition Form be sent to them. The deadline for filing a petition is June 30. The Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the remission compensation process. “Victims are at the core of everything we do at the Department of Justice,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division. “As we did in this complex investment fraud case, the Department pursues forfeiture to take the profit out of crime and then use that money to compensate victims wherever possible. I commend the efforts of our colleagues in the Southern District of New York, our law enforcement partners, and our Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, which manages the Asset Forfeiture Program, for all of their work on behalf of the victims in this important case.” “Between 2014 and 2019, OneCoin’s founders sold a lie disguised as cryptocurrency, costing victims more than $4 billion worldwide,” said U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton for the Southern District of New York. “Today’s announcement marks an important step toward returning funds to those harmed. While no recovery can fully undo the damage, our Office will continue working to seize criminal proceeds and prioritize getting money back into the hands of victims. If you believe you may be a victim of OneCoin, you may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com.” “The victim losses accrued in this case are monumental,” said Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr of the FBI New York Field Office. “Misled by falsified statements and empty promises, many unknowingly depleted their savings for a fraudulent investment scheme in an emerging financial ecosystem that would never pay out. With the unwavering support from the Department of Justice, the FBI maintains its commitment to returning these stolen funds to their rightful owners. Our office will continue its investigative pursuit of these criminal fraudsters — especially locating Ruja Ignatova, an FBI Top Ten Fugitive — alongside our partners at the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) and the Southern District of New York. Any information concerning this fugitive can be submitted online at tips.fbi.gov or via our tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI.” “The victims of the OneCoin scheme were misled and financially devastated by promises that were never real,” said Special Agent in Charge Jenifer L. Piovesan of IRS-CI. “Alongside our law enforcement partners, we worked tirelessly to trace illicit funds and recover them for victims. This compensation process represents a critical step toward returning stolen assets to those who were deceived. IRS-CI remains steadfast in its mission to follow the money and dismantle complex financial fraud schemes like OneCoin.” More information regarding the remission process, including eligibility criteria, updates, and frequently asked questions are available at www.onecoinremission.com or by calling 1-833-421-9748. Kroll Settlement Administration LLC is serving as the remission administrator in this matter. The FBI and IRS-CI conducted the criminal fraud investigation. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs (OIA) provided significant assistance. The Department of Justice, through the Asset Forfeiture Program, works diligently to compensate victims of crime. Since 2000, the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF), which oversees the Asset Forfeiture Program’s victim compensation program, has returned more than $12.5 billion in forfeited assets to victims of crime. MNF Attorney Advisor Drew Halter with the section’s Program Management and Training Unit is leading the remission process. Neither the Remission Administrator nor the Department of Justice will ask for any payment to participate in this remission process. Please be cautious of any individual or organization claiming to represent the Remission Administrator or the federal government in this matter. If you are a victim, any communications will come directly from the Remission Administrator or from government representatives with whom you have already had contact. In addition to his 20-year prison term, Greenwood was ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. According to the DOJ, Breaux and his co-defendants obtained personal identifying information of other inmates, as well as patients and customers at hospitals, dentists’ offices, and other businesses where one of the co-defendants worked or had connections. Breaux and his co-defendants then used this information to submit fraudulent unemployment insurance claims to the California Employment Development Department (EDD). In connection with these false claims, Breaux and his co-defendants also made specific misrepresentations that the individuals whose information they stole were unable to work as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. In total, defendants are alleged to have submitted over 400 fraudulent claims totaling over $25 million to the EDD, $5.4 million of which was actually paid out and used by the defendants to purchase luxury vehicles, fund trips to Las Vegas, and pay rent and tuition. Each defendant faces a maximum of 22 years imprisonment as well as fines of $250,000. A link to the DOJ’s press release can be found here. Former NYC Non-Profit Finance Director Sentenced to 18 Months Imprisonment Donna Murray, the former finance director of a New York City-based nonprofit financial services trade association with over 600 members, was sentenced to 18 months imprisonment for allegedly embezzling nearly half a million dollars from the nonprofit. The government alleges that Murray was the nonprofit’s sole finance department employee and was responsible for maintaining the organization’s books and records, handling accounts receivable and payable, and managing financial statements to outside auditors. In addition, Murray is alleged to have been the only employee with the ability to make wire transfers for the organization. As detailed in the DOJ’s information, Murray was charged with a months-long embezzlement scheme in which she stole over $488,000 from the organization’s bank accounts through 105 unauthorized wire transfers to her personal account. Murray covered up the scheme by creating false entries in the organizations general ledger and transferring less than $10,000 in each transaction to avoid triggering bank reporting requirements. Prosecutors charged Murray with using the misappropriated funds to pay personal loans and purchase luxury items. For her conduct, Murray was sentenced to 18 months in prison. Benefits DOJ Vacancies Legal Careers at DOJ Our Offices Find Help Contact Us Search Breadcrumb Justice.gov Office of Public Affairs News Press Releases Justice Department Announces Compensation Process For OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture MENU News All News Blogs Photo Galleries Podcasts Press Releases Speeches Videos Archived Press Releases Archived News Press Release Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture Monday, April 13, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Today, the Department of Justice announced the beginning of the remission compensation process to provide recovery for victims of the international investment scheme involving OneCoin Ltd. Between 2014 and 2019, Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood, co-founders of OneCoin Ltd. (OneCoin), and others orchestrated a large, international cryptocurrency investment scheme defrauding investors from around the globe. OneCoin, which began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria, marketed and sold a fraudulent cryptocurrency by the same name through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. As a result of misrepresentations made about OneCoin, victims invested over $4 billion worldwide in the fraudulent cryptocurrency. The Department of Justice filed a number of OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York. Several key figures involved in the scheme have been sentenced, and the Department pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the proceeds of the fraud scheme. More than $40 million in forfeited assets are currently available for victim compensation. Through the remission process, victims who purchased the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency between 2014 and 2019 may be eligible for compensation. Individuals who believe they may be victims may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com . Victims may also call, email, or write to the Remission Administrator to request that a Petition Form be sent to them. The deadline for filing a petition is June 30. The Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the remission compensation process. “Victims are at the core of everything we do at the Department of Justice,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division. “As we did in this complex investment fraud case, the Department pursues forfeiture to take the profit out of crime and then use that money to compensate victims wherever possible. I commend the efforts of our colleagues in the Southern District of New York, our law enforcement partners, and our Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, which manages the Asset Forfeiture Program, for all of their work on behalf of the victims in this important case.” “Between 2014 and 2019, OneCoin’s founders sold a lie disguised as cryptocurrency, costing victims more than $4 billion worldwide,” said U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton for the Southern District of New York. “Today’s announcement marks an important step toward returning funds to those harmed. While no recovery can fully undo the damage, our Office will continue working to seize criminal proceeds and prioritize getting money back into the hands of victims. If you believe you may be a victim of OneCoin, you may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com.” “The victim losses accrued in this case are monumental,” said Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr of the FBI New York Field Office. “Misled by falsified statements and empty promises, many unknowingly depleted their savings for a fraudulent investment scheme in an emerging financial ecosystem that would never pay out. With the unwavering support from the Department of Justice, the FBI maintains its commitment to returning these stolen funds to their rightful owners. Our office will continue its investigative pursuit of these criminal fraudsters — especially locating Ruja Ignatova, an FBI Top Ten Fugitive — alongside our partners at the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) and the Southern District of New York. Any information concerning this fugitive can be submitted online at tips.fbi.gov or via our tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI.” “The victims of the OneCoin scheme were misled and financially devastated by promises that were never real,” said Special Agent in Charge Jenifer L. Piovesan of IRS-CI. “Alongside our law enforcement partners, we worked tirelessly to trace illicit funds and recover them for victims. This compensation process represents a critical step toward returning stolen assets to those who were deceived. IRS-CI remains steadfast in its mission to follow the money and dismantle complex financial fraud schemes like OneCoin.” More information regarding the remission process, including eligibility criteria, updates, and frequently asked questions are available at www.onecoinremission.com or by calling 1-833-421-9748. Kroll Settlement Administration LLC is serving as the remission administrator in this matter. The FBI and IRS-CI conducted the criminal fraud investigation. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs (OIA) provided significant assistance. The Department of Justice, through the Asset Forfeiture Program, works diligently to compensate victims of crime. Since 2000, the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF), which oversees the Asset Forfeiture Program’s victim compensation program, has returned more than $12.5 billion in forfeited assets to victims of crime. MNF Attorney Advisor Drew Halter with the section’s Program Management and Training Unit is leading the remission process. Neither the Remission Administrator nor the Department of Justice will ask for any payment to participate in this remission process. Please be cautious of any individual or organization claiming to represent the Remission Administrator or the federal government in this matter. If you are a victim, any communications will come directly from the Remission Administrator or from government representatives with whom you have already had contact.
